label: fiction
title: The Alibi That Spoke
setting: The fictional present-day State of Orinth is led by First Councillor Ilyra Senn. At 2:00, Senn was addressing flood recovery in a secured civic venue. Corin Vale, whose studio had proposed a synthetic-media security demonstration, spoke at a separate luncheon. Event officer Jori Dane admitted a package after a video call appeared to come from Corin. Protective officers isolated it before an activation command could reach it.
charge: attempting a terrorist assassination of the head of government
elements: The accused intended to kill the fictional head of government.
The accused took an act that went beyond mere preparation.
The accused intended the attack to intimidate the public or coerce the fictional government for an ideological purpose.
hook: A live call bearing Corin Vale’s face clears a delivery into First Councillor Ilyra Senn’s venue. At the same minute, Corin is speaking before a luncheon audience elsewhere. The call is synthetic. The jury must decide who controlled what happened next.

accused.human: Corin Vale, 39, runs a civic-media studio and teaches public institutions how synthetic images undermine trust. Corin worked with contractor Daro Quill and two employees on proposed demonstration Second Presence. Jori knew Corin through venue planning. Corin held no official role in Senn’s protective team.
accused.if_guilty: Any sentence is a matter for the judge after the verdict and must play no part in the jury’s decision.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: Corin Vale is charged as the principal—the person who personally sent the activation command—not as someone responsible for Jori Dane or another collaborator. The parties agree an explosive charge entered the venue and somebody tried to activate it. Identity and intent are disputed. You’ll hear from Jori, the investigator who preserved the records, and an examiner who compared two separate digital systems. Judge each source within its limits, then consider whether they converge on Corin and prove the lethal and ideological purpose charged.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: A dangerous event occurred, and Jori wrongly bypassed inspection. Neither fact identifies Corin. Four people could use Second Presence and its administrator account. Daro Quill had carried the stage bag and knew the approval routine. A token record identifies a device, not the hand touching it. Jori first denied receiving an instruction and changed that account after immunity. Corin’s writing describes a risk for a proposed safety exercise. Keep each record within its proved limits and ask whether another authorised collaborator remains reasonably possible.

prosecution.speaker: pc
prosecution.text: The shared archive cannot identify its operator; the prosecution accepts that. Now assemble the independent chronology. Jori says Corin arranged the false approval and bypass. At 2:06 the provider issued a fresh challenge, Corin’s token confirmed it, and the command followed. Certified footage places Corin with the bag from 2:04 to 2:07. The device was real, the exercise unapproved, and Corin’s admitted scenario contemplated public fear forcing a change in government power. Those circumstances prove Corin personally attempted the ideologically motivated killing.

defence.speaker: dc
defence.text: That chronology contains a human gap. The token records no fingerprint, the side entrance was unfilmed, and Daro had carried the bag and knew its approval routine. The project, deletion queue, recordings, and code were shared. Jori changed accounts after immunity and never heard Corin mention violence or politics. Corin’s draft warns what a borrowed face might cause; it does not request an attack. The defence need not prove Daro acted. Unless the prosecution excludes that reasonable access and proves Corin’s lethal and ideological intent, the verdict is Not Guilty.

epilogue: Ilyra Senn later completed the flood-recovery address from a smaller civic hall and commissioned an independent review of synthetic authorisation at public venues. Jori Dane left events work after acknowledging the inspection bypass. Corin Vale’s teaching materials remained sealed with the trial exhibits while former students argued over whether the lessons had been misused or misunderstood. The venue replaced face-and-voice approvals with two-person confirmation, and the luncheon recording continued to circulate as a reminder that a genuine appearance can coexist with a false one.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: The parties agree no Orinth office authorised Second Presence that day. Corin’s proposal remained unapproved, venue staff received no exercise notice, and the package was a real device, not a training item. They also agree the call used the studio project, four people shared its account, and Corin’s token confirmed the later challenge. Those matters are proved. The parties dispute who operated the project, who touched the token, what Corin intended, and whether someone else could reach the bag. The agreements do not decide those questions.
beats.reveal_note: The agreed records answered the claim of an authorised exercise but expressly left personal attribution to the other evidence.

beats.speaker: judge
beats.text: Under Orinth law, Corin is alleged to be the principal who personally sent the command, not responsible for another person. An attempt requires an act beyond preparation. Sending a command may qualify despite intervention, but only if Corin sent it. You must be sure Corin intended to kill Ilyra Senn and intended public intimidation or government coercion for an ideological purpose. Professional interest, criticism, or reform is not enough. Consider the evidence together, respecting each record’s limits and Jori’s immunity. Corin need not identify another operator. If you are not sure the prosecution proved every element beyond reasonable doubt, your verdict must be Not Guilty. Do not consider punishment or research the case.
beats.reveal_note: The direction confines liability to Corin’s alleged personal activation and prevents project ownership, ambiguous writing, or another person’s conduct from replacing proof.

twist: The authors’ intended resolution is Guilty on principal liability, not because Corin owned a synthetic-media studio. The central inference is that Corin’s registered key was freshly confirmed while certified footage placed the key and Corin together during the activation window; Jori’s advance instruction and the unapproved risk scenario support intent. The strongest reasonable opposing interpretation is that Daro used shared project access and briefly reached the bag through the unfilmed side entrance, while Corin’s writing described a legitimate safety demonstration.

jurors.label: Juror 2 — Anya
jurors.persona: Anya’s first reaction is that a stolen face must mean a frame, but she can revise a vivid impression.

agree: The fake call could be a frame, and four people could use the source archive. Isn’t that real doubt?
pushback: But the fake call isn’t the activation command. What do we do with the key in Corin’s bag?
concede: Wait—the fresh key approval changes my first reaction. The copied face isn’t the only identity evidence.
burden_drift: I keep wanting Corin to explain every studio file because the work feels suspicious.
burden_correct: No, shared access means the prosecution needs a separate link to Corin personally.
final: I stopped treating the fake face as the answer and decided on the key evidence.

jurors.label: Juror 3 — Bex
jurors.persona: Bex focuses on who gave each instruction and refuses to merge Jori’s conduct with Corin’s.

agree: Jori says Corin supplied the exact code and told her to skip the second officer. That matters.
pushback: I don’t trust Jori’s later memory on its own. What backs it up?
concede: The key record is separate from Jori and points to Corin during the command window.
burden_drift: Jori broke the rule, and I catch myself asking Corin to prove Jori acted alone.
burden_correct: Let’s keep them separate: the prosecution must prove Corin’s own activation.
final: I relied on Corin’s personal command, not guilt by association with Jori.

jurors.label: Juror 4 — Cora
jurors.persona: Cora will not let the seriousness of the prevented attack lower the standard or blur personal identity.

agree: The attack was real and grave. That still doesn’t tell us whose hand confirmed the key.
pushback: An ambiguous safety draft cannot repair weak identity evidence.
concede: I accept the timing is unusually tight: Corin, the bag, the fresh prompt, and the command all meet at 2:06.
burden_drift: The avoided harm makes an uncertain inference feel easier than it should.
burden_correct: Every element still needs proof beyond reasonable doubt, including Corin’s personal act.
final: For me, the independently certified timing finally crossed the burden.

jurors.label: Juror 5 — Dev
jurors.persona: Dev begins with the shared-access defence and changes only if another record attributes the decisive act.

agree: The administrator log genuinely can’t distinguish four authorised people. We shouldn’t pretend it can.
pushback: Shared project access answers the call project, but does it answer the separate key?
concede: I’ve changed my view. The fresh prompt prevents Daro from preparing the activation earlier.
burden_drift: A pile of matching records can make me overlook which one actually identifies a person.
burden_correct: The prosecution needs a trace to Corin’s own act, not just to Corin’s business.
final: The project remained shared; the activation key and timing did not.

jurors.label: Juror 6 — Esra
jurors.persona: Esra keeps the discussion on Corin’s alleged personal act and asks the room to name its source.

agree: We agree an activation was attempted. Can we now focus on who personally confirmed it?
pushback: The draft speaks about a risk. Where’s the proof that Corin wanted that risk to happen?
concede: The key timing answers identity for me; the unapproved device and admitted policy goal answer intent together.
burden_drift: We’re drifting toward asking Corin to identify whoever used the side entrance.
burden_correct: Corin doesn’t have to name another operator. The prosecution has to make us sure it was Corin.
final: I checked the personal act first, then intent, instead of letting the event decide for me.

jurors.label: Juror 7 — Fia
jurors.persona: Fia is strongly influenced by Corin’s simultaneous luncheon appearance until the room separates call creation from activation.

agree: Corin is onstage during the fake call. I know that’s not a complete alibi, but it still matters.
pushback: Are we sure the person in the greenroom was alone, or only that the hallway camera saw one person?
concede: I was letting the luncheon image control everything. Corin could be onstage at two and use the key at 2:06.
burden_drift: Corin’s expertise makes me want proof that no collaborator copied anything.
burden_correct: That’s wrong. The prosecution must prove Corin used this key for this command.
final: The public appearance didn’t answer what happened six minutes later.

jurors.label: Juror 8 — Garen
jurors.persona: Garen distinguishes the shared synthetic-media work from the later human decision to activate the device.

agree: The expert proved the call archive was shared. The activation key is a different system and a different question.
pushback: A shared login means we can’t attribute the project activity to Corin. I won’t pretend otherwise.
concede: I accept that the key doesn’t record a fingerprint, but the fresh prompt sharply limits who could use it.
burden_drift: Technical complexity can make Corin’s innocent explanation feel like a duty.
burden_correct: We should rely on proved limits and links, not demand a complete production history from Corin.
final: I treated the project attribution as unresolved and the activation attribution as proved.

jurors.label: Juror 9 — Hale
jurors.persona: Hale distrusts immunity evidence and asks whether independent records confirm the precise part Jori added later.

agree: Jori changed the story after immunity, and Daro knew the code too. We can’t skip that.
pushback: Maybe Jori is telling the truth now, but which record confirms Corin gave the instruction?
concede: The key doesn’t prove Jori’s words, but it independently connects Corin to the later command.
burden_drift: I almost asked Corin to prove Jori and Daro acted together. That isn’t Corin’s burden.
burden_correct: We have to test Jori against independent evidence, not against Corin’s ability to solve the case.
final: I used Jori cautiously and reached identity through the separate key record.

jurors.label: Juror 10 — Iri
jurors.persona: Iri reacts strongly to the inspection bypass and has to correct a tendency to treat ownership as control.

agree: Jori says Corin set up the bypass before the fake call. That’s a direct accusation.
pushback: Daro knew the code and carried the bag. Why isn’t that enough for doubt?
